key_claims: Episodic memory decline in ageing is typically attributed to the cortico-hippocampal system, but the cerebellar contribution via cerebellar-cerebral circuits is underexplored.

Using task-based fMRI data from 821 older adults, including a longitudinal subset of 78 participants followed for four years, three non-motor cerebellar networks were identified: a bilateral lobule VI/Crus I mnemonic monitoring network, a right lobule Crus I/II default mode aligned network, and a right lobule VIIb/VIIIa evidence evaluation network.
Network recruitment varied with task demands and was associated with memory performance.
Phase-specific static cerebellar-cerebral functional connectivity showed stable organization but limited behavioural specificity.
Dynamic functional connectivity patterns effectively distinguished memory performance groups.
Greater instability in dynamic functional connectivity during encoding predicted longitudinal retrieval slowing.
limitations: The study is based on a specific sample of older adults and may not generalize to other populations.
The longitudinal subset is small (78 participants) relative to the full sample.
The study is observational and cannot establish causality.
The source does not provide effect sizes or statistical details.
what_not_to_say: The study proves that cerebellar networks cause episodic memory decline.
The study provides a clinical intervention or treatment for memory decline.
The study identifies specific genes or molecular mechanisms.
The study shows that static functional connectivity is not important for memory.
The study claims that all older adults show the same pattern of network instability.
